title: Password Security Audit Checklist: 20 Things to Check Right Now
excerpt: A practical, step-by-step security audit you can complete in an afternoon. Work through this checklist to find and fix the vulnerabilities in your current password setup.
content:
Why You Need a Password Security Audit

Most people's password security has gaps they're not aware of: an old account still using 'password123', a former email address that gets password resets for important accounts, two-factor authentication disabled on their most sensitive accounts. A security audit finds these gaps before an attacker does.

This checklist is designed to be completed in roughly 2-3 hours. Work through it systematically and fix issues as you find them. Use our password generator to create replacements for any weak passwords you find.

Section 1: Password Strength and Uniqueness

  1. Export and review your passwords. In Chrome: go to passwords.google.com and click 'Checkup.' In Firefox: Settings → Passwords → 'Check for breaches.' In Safari: Settings → Passwords → tap the security recommendations. In your password manager: run the built-in security audit (1Password's Watchtower, NordPass's Data Breach Scanner, Bitwarden's Health Reports).
  2. Identify reused passwords. Every account with a reused password is a single point of failure. List them out. Your goal: zero reused passwords.
  3. Identify weak passwords. Flag any password under 12 characters, any password that's a word or simple pattern, any password that includes your name, birthday, or other personal information.
  4. Prioritize what to fix first. Rank your accounts by damage potential: email (highest), banking/financial, work accounts, social media, shopping accounts, entertainment (lowest). Fix in that order.
  5. Replace weak and reused passwords. For each flagged account, log in and change the password. Use your password generator set to at least 20 characters with all character types enabled. Let your password manager save it automatically.

Section 2: Two-Factor Authentication

  1. Check which accounts have 2FA enabled. Go through your most important accounts and verify 2FA status. Most platforms show this under Settings → Security.
  2. Enable 2FA on all accounts that offer it. Absolute minimum: email, banking, password manager, social media, work accounts, any account storing payment information.
  3. Upgrade SMS 2FA to authenticator app 2FA where possible. Go through any account where you set up SMS 2FA and check if an authenticator app option is also available. Authenticator apps can't be intercepted via SIM swapping.
  4. Save or regenerate backup codes. For each account with 2FA, find the backup codes (usually in Security settings). Store them in your password manager. Print a set for your most critical accounts.
  5. Test your 2FA. Log out and log back in to confirm 2FA is working correctly before you forget the backup codes.

Section 3: Recovery Settings

  1. Audit recovery email addresses. For each important account, check what email address is set as the recovery address. Ensure you still control it and that it's also secured with a strong password and 2FA.
  2. Audit recovery phone numbers. Check which phone number is linked to each account. If a number is for a phone you no longer have, update it.
  3. Review security questions. Security questions are often the weakest link — the answers are frequently guessable or findable on social media. If an account uses security questions, use random answers (generate them like passwords) and store those answers in your password manager notes.
  4. Check active sessions and connected apps. In each major account (Google, Facebook, Microsoft, Apple), look for 'Active sessions' or 'Connected apps.' Log out everything you don't recognize. Remove any third-party app you no longer use.

Section 4: Breach Exposure

  1. Check your email addresses on Have I Been Pwned. Go to haveibeenpwned.com and enter every email address you use. It shows you which data breaches your email appeared in and what data was exposed. If your email appears in a breach that included passwords, change any matching password immediately.
  2. Check your phone number too. HaveIBeenPwned also accepts phone numbers now. Enter yours in E.164 format (e.g., +15551234567).
  3. Set up breach monitoring. Sign up for breach alerts so you're notified when your email appears in future breaches. HIBP offers a free notification service.

Section 5: Device and Storage Security

  1. Check how your devices autofill passwords. If you're relying on Chrome, Firefox, or Safari's built-in password storage without a master password protecting it, anyone who picks up your unlocked device has access to all your saved passwords. Consider migrating to a dedicated password manager with its own master password and auto-lock.
  2. Review any physical password records. If you have passwords written on sticky notes or in a notebook, assess the risk. A locked safe is fine. A notebook next to your computer is not. If you must write passwords down, keep them in a private location and don't label them obviously.
  3. Check password manager security settings. Ensure your password manager is set to: lock after 5 minutes of inactivity, require biometric or master password to unlock, and has 2FA enabled on its own account.

Scheduling Your Next Audit

A password security audit should happen at least once a year — set a calendar reminder. You should also trigger an immediate mini-audit whenever: you get a breach notification for any service you use, you hear about a major breach at a company (even if you're unsure if you're affected), you lose or sell a device, or you leave a job.

Recommended Tools

The easiest way to run an ongoing audit is with a password manager that includes health monitoring. NordPass Premium includes Data Breach Scanner and a Password Health report. 1Password's Watchtower feature provides continuous monitoring with color-coded alerts.
